items.definition: A file sent together with the email. It should be named clearly and referred to in the body.
items.example: Please find the attachment, called Quotation-March-2026.pdf.

items.definition: The set of assumptions a person carries about how other people answer when they reach out.
items.example: My working model says that people get busy and come back, so I wait.

items.definition: The person or relationship a person can move away from and still feel steady in.
items.example: His sister was his secure base long before he had a partner of his own.

items.definition: The event that makes a person read a partner as less available than the person assumed.
items.example: One missed call was the trigger, and the rest of the evening went into reading the silence.

items.definition: Describing a person who takes the partner's availability for granted and stays steady when it wobbles.
items.example: She is secure with him, so she says she is upset instead of guessing.

items.definition: Describing a person who reads any drop in a partner's availability as a sign that the bond is at risk.
items.example: When he was busy, his anxious side read the quiet as a message about him.

items.definition: Describing a person who leans away when closeness increases, to protect independence.
items.example: His avoidant side called for less contact at the moment he needed it most.

items.definition: Describing a person who wants closeness and is afraid of it at the same time.
items.example: Fearful-avoidant behaviour often looks like pulling back right after reaching out.

items.definition: The rising of the alarm when a partner seems unavailable, which sharpens attention and speeds the urge to act.
items.example: Hyperactivation turned three unanswered messages into an hour of checking the phone.

items.definition: The lowering of the alarm when closeness increases, which turns attention away from the bond and towards the task in front of it.
items.example: Deactivation looked like a tidy desk and a long shift at the office.

items.definition: Asking a partner repeatedly to confirm that the relationship is still there.
items.example: Reassurance-seeking is asking the same question until the answer changes.

items.definition: The behaviour a person uses to get a partner's attention back when they feel the bond is slipping.
items.example: Her protest behaviour was sending the message twice and then three times.

items.definition: Pulling back from a partner and reducing contact when closeness or conflict increases.
items.example: Withdrawal is answering with less, not more, when the other person asks for more.

items.definition: The capacity to feel safe in a relationship, learned later in life rather than carried in from earlier life.
items.example: Her earned security came from a relationship that stayed, after years of ones that did not.

items.definition: The phrase for the idea that time passes in the body as well as in the calendar, and that a window is closing.
items.example: The biological clock is a phrase, and the window it names is mostly a story.

items.definition: The way the reproductive system changes as a person gets older.
items.example: Reproductive ageing is gradual, and it is not the same for everybody.

items.definition: The stretch of future time a person is thinking about when they make a plan.
items.example: Their time horizon was ten years ahead; mine was two.

items.definition: The capacity to reproduce, which changes across the life span.
items.example: Fertility is not a number that stays the same for a whole life.

items.definition: The chance that conception happens in one cycle.
items.example: Fecundity is the word for the chance in a single cycle.

items.definition: An estimate of how many eggs remain in the ovaries, built from hormone measurements and sometimes a scan.
items.example: The ovarian reserve estimate describes a stock; it is not a statement about the odds.

items.definition: The point at which ovulation and menstruation stop.
items.example: Menopause is a biological event, not a date on a calendar.

items.definition: The transition before menopause, when the cycles often change.
items.example: She was in perimenopause, and her cycles had changed for a while.

items.definition: The age of the woman when her child is born, used as a medical label.
items.example: Maternal age is a label in the record, not a judgement about the mother.

items.definition: The age of the father when his child is born, used as a medical label.
items.example: Paternal age carries different facts from maternal age, and the change is slower.

items.definition: The felt push to act on reproduction because the window seems to be closing.
items.example: The reproductive urgency was real, and the deadline behind it was still unchecked.

items.definition: Pressure that comes from a deadline somebody else has set.
items.example: The timeline pressure came from the family, not from her body.

items.definition: An expectation that one generation passes to the next about when life should happen.
items.example: Generational pressure rarely sounds like a command; it sounds like an observation.

items.definition: A line you draw around your time, energy, body or values, and say out loud so other people can respect it.
items.example: Her boundary was simple: no phone calls after ten.

items.definition: The point at which you stop giving: the time, the amount or the effort. A limit is the measurable side of a boundary.
items.example: My limit is two favours a week, and I stick to it.

items.definition: Something a person asks of you. A request deserves an answer; it does not deserve obedience.
items.example: The request was reasonable, and the answer was still no.

items.definition: To have to have something.
The act of saying no to something. It is a decision about an offer, not a verdict on a person.
items.example: She declined the invitation politely and without drama.

items.definition: The result you decide to bring about when a boundary is crossed. It is chosen by you, and it should be small and repeatable.
items.example: Her consequence was simple: she stopped answering messages late at night.

items.definition: An intense feeling of attraction for someone you have not yet got close to.
items.example: I have a crush on someone from my office, but we have only ever said hello.

items.definition: A planned meeting with someone you are getting to know. It implies time set aside for each other.
items.example: Is Friday a date, or just a coffee between friends?

items.definition: A relationship that has no agreed label. Nobody has said what it is, and nobody has asked.
items.example: We have been seeing each other for months and calling it a situationship.

items.definition: Stopping all contact without explanation, so the other person is left waiting and guessing.
items.example: He replied for three weeks and then ghosted me completely.

items.definition: Sending occasional messages to keep someone interested while never making any real plan.
items.example: He messages me every few days but has never once suggested meeting.

items.definition: Someone you were in a relationship with and are no longer in one.
items.example: My ex and I still share a group of friends, so we keep it simple.

items.definition: When one person's behaviour and words point in different directions, usually because they are unsure or unwilling to say where things stand.
items.example: He texts every day but has cancelled three plans — those are mixed signals.
